claim: Pulmonary tuberculosis is characterized by the formation of macrophage-rich granulomas.
source: A hallmark of pulmonary tuberculosis is the formation of macrophage-rich granulomas.
evidence: This is a well-established characteristic of tuberculosis supported by scientific literature.

claim: Granulomas may restrict Mycobacterium tuberculosis growth or progress to central necrosis and cavitation.
source: These may restrict Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) growth, or progress to central necrosis and cavitation, facilitating pathogen growth.
evidence: This statement is supported by established knowledge about tuberculosis pathology.

claim: Internalization of Mtb aggregates caused macrophage death.
source: Internalization of Mtb aggregates caused macrophage death, and phagocytosis of large aggregates was more cytotoxic than multiple small aggregates containing similar numbers of bacilli.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations from live cell imaging experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: Phagocytosis of large aggregates was more cytotoxic than multiple small aggregates containing similar numbers of bacilli.
source: Internalization of Mtb aggregates caused macrophage death, and phagocytosis of large aggregates was more cytotoxic than multiple small aggregates containing similar numbers of bacilli.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing death frequencies between different internalization patterns as shown in Figure 2.

claim: Macrophage death did not result in clearance of Mtb.
source: Macrophage death did not result in clearance of Mtb.
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations showing Mtb survival and growth after macrophage death.

claim: Macrophage death led to accelerated intracellular Mtb growth regardless of prior activation or macrophage type.
source: Rather, it led to accelerated intracellular Mtb growth regardless of prior activation or macrophage type.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from IFNγ-treated MDM and alveolar macrophages shown in Figure 7.

claim: Bacillary replication was controlled in live phagocytes.
source: In contrast, bacillary replication was controlled in live phagocytes.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing minimal growth in live cells compared to dead cells as shown in Figure 6.

claim: Mtb grew as a clump in dead cells.
source: Mtb grew as a clump in dead cells, and macrophages which internalized dead infected cells were very likely to die themselves, leading to a cell death cascade.
evidence: This is supported by microscopy observations shown in Figure 5 and Video 5.

claim: Macrophages which internalized dead infected cells were very likely to die themselves.
source: Mtb grew as a clump in dead cells, and macrophages which internalized dead infected cells were very likely to die themselves, leading to a cell death cascade.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing 89% death frequency in cells that internalized dead infected cells as shown in Figure 8.

claim: Granulomas have a defined anatomical structure as well as segregated expression of immune system related proteins within the structure.
source: Granulomas, which have a defined anatomical structure as well as segregated expression of immune system related proteins within the structure (Marakalala et al., 2016), differentiate and mature independent of each other in infected tissues, most often the lung.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Marakalala et al., 2016.

claim: Granulomas differentiate and mature independent of each other in infected tissues, most often the lung.
source: Granulomas, which have a defined anatomical structure as well as segregated expression of immune system related proteins within the structure (Marakalala et al., 2016), differentiate and mature independent of each other in infected tissues, most often the lung.
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge about granuloma biology.

claim: Pulmonary granuloma formation is driven by macrophage phagocytosis of inhaled, viable Mtb.
source: The process of pulmonary granuloma formation is driven by macrophage phagocytosis of inhaled, viable Mtb, followed by extravasation of monocytes and T cells from the circulation and their accumulation at the site of infection (Ramakrishnan, 2012; Russell, 2007; Russell et al., 2010; Barry et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to the literature.

claim: Different granulomas in the same lung can control the infection or support the growth of the bacilli.
source: However, granulomas do not always succeed in containing Mtb infection, and different granulomas in the same lung can control the infection or support the growth of the bacilli (Barry et al., 2009; Lenaerts et al., 2015; Lin et al., 2014; Kaplan et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to the literature.

claim: Central necrosis within the granuloma, cavity formation, and breach into the airways results in release of Mtb into the environment and transmission of the infection to another human host.
source: In the latter case, central necrosis within the granuloma, cavity formation, and breach into the airways, results in release of Mtb into the environment and transmission of the infection to another human host (Ramakrishnan, 2012; Russell, 2007; Russell et al., 2010; Barry et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to the literature.

claim: Mtb proliferation during active pulmonary tuberculosis occurs in an environment containing many dead cells and cell remnants.
source: Thus, while Mtb is considered an intracellular pathogen infecting live cells, its proliferation during active pulmonary tuberculosis occurs in an environment containing many dead cells and cell remnants (Kaplan et al., 2003; Hunter, 2011; Hunter et al., 2007; Welsh et al., 2011; Irwin et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to the literature.

claim: Apoptosis was reported to be protective against Mtb.
source: Apoptosis was reported to be protective against Mtb (Fratazzi et al., 1999; Gan et al., 2008; Keane et al., 2000; Molloy et al., 1994; Oddo et al., 1998; Behar et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to the literature.

claim: Protection from apoptosis is mediated through efferocytosis, the internalization of apoptotic cell fragments by macrophages, leading to the elimination of the Mtb inside the cellular fragments.
source: Evidence from mouse macrophages shows that protection is mediated through efferocytosis, the internalization of apoptotic cell fragments by macrophages, leading to the elimination of the Mtb inside the cellular fragments (Martin et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Martin et al., 2012.

claim: Mtb was not killed when necrotic cell death was induced by H2O2.
source: Mtb was not killed when necrotic cell death was induced by H2O2 (Molloy et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Molloy et al., 1994.

claim: Mtb initiates non-apoptotic cell death by the breakdown of mitochondrial membrane integrity.
source: Mtb is reported to initiate non-apoptotic cell death by the breakdown of mitochondrial membrane integrity (Duan et al., 2002), interference with host plasma membrane repair through inhibition of prostaglandin E2 (Divangahi et al., 2009; Divangahi et al., 2010), and secretion of a necrosis inducing toxin which kills macrophages by hydrolyzing NAD (Sun et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Duan et al., 2002.

claim: Mtb interferes with host plasma membrane repair through inhibition of prostaglandin E2.
source: Mtb is reported to initiate non-apoptotic cell death by the breakdown of mitochondrial membrane integrity (Duan et al., 2002), interference with host plasma membrane repair through inhibition of prostaglandin E2 (Divangahi et al., 2009; Divangahi et al., 2010), and secretion of a necrosis inducing toxin which kills macrophages by hydrolyzing NAD (Sun et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Divangahi et al., 2009 and 2010.

claim: Mtb secretes a necrosis inducing toxin which kills macrophages by hydrolyzing NAD.
source: Mtb is reported to initiate non-apoptotic cell death by the breakdown of mitochondrial membrane integrity (Duan et al., 2002), interference with host plasma membrane repair through inhibition of prostaglandin E2 (Divangahi et al., 2009; Divangahi et al., 2010), and secretion of a necrosis inducing toxin which kills macrophages by hydrolyzing NAD (Sun et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Sun et al., 2015.

claim: Mtb infection is controlled by the adaptive immune response.
source: Mtb infection is known to be controlled by the adaptive immune response (Cooper and Flynn, 1995; Flynn et al., 1995, 1992) which becomes effective several weeks after exposure (Wolf et al., 2008), though a study using intravital imaging observed limited T cell effector function in Mtb granulomas (Egen et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to the literature.

claim: The adaptive immune response becomes effective several weeks after exposure.
source: Mtb infection is known to be controlled by the adaptive immune response (Cooper and Flynn, 1995; Flynn et al., 1995, 1992) which becomes effective several weeks after exposure (Wolf et al., 2008), though a study using intravital imaging observed limited T cell effector function in Mtb granulomas (Egen et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Wolf et al., 2008.

claim: A study using intravital imaging observed limited T cell effector function in Mtb granulomas.
source: Mtb infection is known to be controlled by the adaptive immune response (Cooper and Flynn, 1995; Flynn et al., 1995, 1992) which becomes effective several weeks after exposure (Wolf et al., 2008), though a study using intravital imaging observed limited T cell effector function in Mtb granulomas (Egen et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Egen et al., 2011.

claim: The adaptive immune response controls Mtb by activating macrophages with factors such as interferon gamma (IFNγ) to kill or control the growth of the bacilli.
source: The adaptive immune response controls Mtb by activating macrophages with factors such as interferon gamma (IFNγ) to kill or control the growth of the bacilli, and by targeting infected macrophages with cytotoxic lymphocytes (Cooper and Flynn, 1995; Flynn et al., 1995, 1992).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to the literature.

claim: Macrophage fate depends on the number of Mtb internalized.
source: Macrophage fate was found to depend on the number of Mtb internalized.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: As the number of bacteria internalized increased, there was more cell death and it occurred sooner.
source: As the number of bacteria internalized increased, there was more cell death and it occurred sooner (Figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Phagocytosis of small numbers of Mtb, less than approximately 10 bacilli, did not induce significantly more macrophage death than observed in uninfected bystander cells.
source: Phagocytosis of small numbers of Mtb, less than approximately 10 bacilli, did not induce significantly more macrophage death than observed in uninfected bystander cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: Above 10 Mtb internalized but below approximately 30, there was a trend toward increased macrophage death relative to bystander cells, but the differences in frequencies were not significant.
source: Above 10 Mtb internalized but below approximately 30, there was a trend toward increased macrophage death relative to bystander cells, but the differences in frequencies were not significant (see Figure 1—figure supplement 5B for p-values and significance thresholds).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5B.

claim: The probability of death increased significantly relative to bystanders and cells with less than 10 Mtb when more than 30 Mtb were internalized per cell over the course of the movie.
source: The probability of death increased significantly relative to bystanders and cells with less than 10 Mtb when more than 30 Mtb were internalized per cell over the course of the movie, and a threshold for Mtb to induce death was clearly visible in Figure 1 at about 50 Mtb internalized, with differences relative to bystander and lightly infected cells becoming highly significant (Figure 1—figure supplement 5B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 5B.

claim: A threshold for Mtb to induce death was clearly visible at about 50 Mtb internalized.
source: The probability of death increased significantly relative to bystanders and cells with less than 10 Mtb when more than 30 Mtb were internalized per cell over the course of the movie, and a threshold for Mtb to induce death was clearly visible in Figure 1 at about 50 Mtb internalized, with differences relative to bystander and lightly infected cells becoming highly significant (Figure 1—figure supplement 5B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: There is a tight correspondence between Mtb fluorescence and colony forming units (CFU).
source: We found a tight correspondence between the two measures (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), with an incremental increase in fluorescence translating to an incremental increase in the number of bacilli as measured by CFU.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Fluorescence measurements reflect Mtb numbers and an increase in Mtb fluorescence reflects Mtb growth.
source: Hence, fluorescence measurements reflect Mtb numbers and an increase in Mtb fluorescence reflects Mtb growth.
evidence: This is inferred from the tight correspondence between fluorescence and CFU measurements.

claim: The frequency of cell death was 47% for cells that accumulated Mtb in three or more internalizations.
source: While 47% of the cells died when they accumulated Mtb in three or more internalizations, 71% of the cells died when they internalized a similar mean number of Mtb as one pickup.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: 71% of the cells died when they internalized a similar mean number of Mtb as one pickup.
source: While 47% of the cells died when they accumulated Mtb in three or more internalizations, 71% of the cells died when they internalized a similar mean number of Mtb as one pickup.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The difference in death frequency between multiple pickups and single pickups was significant (p=5×10−4).
source: The difference was significant (p=5×10−4 by bootstrap).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Time to cell death after internalization inversely correlated with the number of bacteria internalized in a single pickup.
source: The time to cell death after internalization inversely correlated with the number of bacteria internalized in a single pickup (Figure 3B, R2 = 0.45, p=2×10−6), indicating that uptake of larger clumps led to faster onset of macrophage death.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Uptake of larger clumps led to faster onset of macrophage death.
source: The time to cell death after internalization inversely correlated with the number of bacteria internalized in a single pickup (Figure 3B, R2 = 0.45, p=2×10−6), indicating that uptake of larger clumps led to faster onset of macrophage death.
evidence: This is inferred from the inverse correlation between time to death and bacterial number.

claim: Mtb typically induced phagocyte cell death with immediate loss of membrane integrity.
source: Mtb typically induced phagocyte cell death with immediate loss of membrane integrity (Video 2, Figure 4), similar to nigericin induced cell death (Video 3, Figure 4), and consistent with a previous study using A549 epithelial cells (Dobos et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Video 2 and Figure 4.

claim: Mtb-induced cell death is similar to nigericin induced cell death.
source: Mtb typically induced phagocyte cell death with immediate loss of membrane integrity (Video 2, Figure 4), similar to nigericin induced cell death (Video 3, Figure 4), and consistent with a previous study using A549 epithelial cells (Dobos et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Videos 2 and 3, and Figure 4.

claim: Cisplatin induced cell death was apparent significantly before incorporation of DRAQ7.
source: In contrast, cisplatin induced cell death was apparent significantly before incorporation of DRAQ7 (Video 4, Figure 4).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Video 4 and Figure 4.

claim: Mtb-induced macrophage death did not lead to the killing of the bacilli.
source: Mtb-induced macrophage death did not lead to the killing of the bacilli, and Mtb fluorescence levels increased in the dead cells (Figure 5A, Video 5).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A and Video 5.

claim: Mtb fluorescence levels increased in the dead cells.
source: Mtb-induced macrophage death did not lead to the killing of the bacilli, and Mtb fluorescence levels increased in the dead cells (Figure 5A, Video 5).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A and Video 5.

claim: Mtb did not burst out of the cell to spread into the neighboring medium.
source: Mtb did not burst out of the cell to spread into the neighboring medium. Instead, the bacilli remained tightly associated with the dead host cell as a growing clump.
evidence: This is supported by microscopy observations.

claim: The bacilli remained tightly associated with the dead host cell as a growing clump.
source: Mtb did not burst out of the cell to spread into the neighboring medium. Instead, the bacilli remained tightly associated with the dead host cell as a growing clump.
evidence: This is supported by microscopy observations.

claim: Out of the 92 dead infected cells evaluated, 90 showed positive growth rates while two had declining Mtb numbers.
source: Out of the 92 dead infected cells we evaluated, 90 showed positive growth rates while two had declining Mtb numbers (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Intracellular Mtb had a median doubling time of 24.7 hr (interquartile range 19 to 34 hr) in dead cells.
source: Intracellular Mtb had a median doubling time, excluding the two negative values, of 24.7 hr (interquartile range 19 to 34 hr, Figure 5B inset).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B inset.

claim: The extracellular growth rate of Mtb had a median doubling time of 36.1 hr (interquartile range 31 to 44 hr).
source: The extracellular growth rate of Mtb in the same experiments had a median doubling time of 36.1 hr (interquartile range 31 to 44 hr, Figure 5B inset), significantly slower than in dead cells (p=7×10−8, Wilcoxon rank sum test).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B inset.

claim: Extracellular Mtb growth was significantly slower than growth in dead cells (p=7×10−8).
source: The extracellular growth rate of Mtb in the same experiments had a median doubling time of 36.1 hr (interquartile range 31 to 44 hr, Figure 5B inset), significantly slower than in dead cells (p=7×10−8, Wilcoxon rank sum test).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Approximately an order of magnitude more Mtb was recovered by CFU after growth in dead cells versus after growth in the MDM extracellular medium.
source: We recovered approximately an order of magnitude more Mtb by CFU after growth in dead cells versus after growth in the MDM extracellular medium (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The median growth constant for Mtb in live cells was 0.0012 hour−1 (interquartile range −0.016 to 0.022), translating to a doubling time of >100 hr.
source: The median growth constant for Mtb in live cells was 0.0012 hour−1 (interquartile range −0.016 to 0.022), translating to a doubling time of >100 hr (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The slope of Mtb growth in live cells was not significantly different from 0 (p=0.3).
source: The slope was not significantly different from 0 (p=0.3, right tailed Sign Test).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: The median growth constant for Mtb in dead cells was 0.033 hour−1 (interquartile range 0.021 to 0.045), translating to a doubling time of 21.2 hr.
source: In contrast, the median growth constant for Mtb in dead cells was 0.033 hour−1 (interquartile range 0.021 to 0.045), translating to a doubling time of 21.2 hr (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Mtb growth in dead cells was positive (p=5×10−23).
source: Mtb growth in dead cells was positive (p=5×10−23, right tailed Sign Test), and significantly faster than in live infected cells (p=8×10−15, Wilcoxon rank sum test).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Mtb growth in dead cells was significantly faster than in live infected cells (p=8×10−15).
source: Mtb growth in dead cells was positive (p=5×10−23, right tailed Sign Test), and significantly faster than in live infected cells (p=8×10−15, Wilcoxon rank sum test).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Mtb were in an acidified compartment in live MDM.
source: We observed that Mtb were in an acidified compartment in live MDM (Video 6 and Figure 6C), with seemingly variable acidification of different bacilli in the same macrophage.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data using pHrodo dye shown in Video 6 and Figure 6C.

claim: Upon Mtb induced MDM death, pHrodo signal was rapidly reduced to near background, indicating that acidification was lost.
source: Upon Mtb induced MDM death, pHrodo signal was rapidly reduced to near background, indicating that acidification was lost (Video 6, Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Video 6 and Figure 6D.

claim: Live infected MDM sequestered Mtb in a phagosomal compartment, which was at least partially acidified.
source: This indicates that live infected MDM sequestered Mtb in a phagosomal compartment, which was at least partially acidified.
evidence: This is inferred from the pHrodo signal data.

claim: Upon cell death, compartmentalization of Mtb disappeared.
source: Upon cell death, this compartmentalization disappeared.
evidence: This is inferred from the loss of pHrodo signal upon cell death.

claim: The median growth constant in dead MDM treated before death with IFNγ was 0.027 hour−1 (interquartile range 0.0076 to 0.046), corresponding to a doubling time of 25.8 hr.
source: The median growth constant in dead MDM treated before death with IFNγ was 0.027 hour−1 (interquartile range 0.0076 to 0.046), corresponding to a doubling time of 25.8 hr.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The median growth constant in dead alveolar macrophages was 0.028 hour−1 (interquartile range 0.0014 to 0.055), corresponding to a doubling time of 24.6 hr.
source: The median growth constant in dead alveolar macrophages was 0.028 hour−1 (interquartile range 0.0014 to 0.055), corresponding to a doubling time of 24.6 hr.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The median growth constant for extracellular Mtb during a ten-hour window was 0.018 hour−1 (interquartile range 0.0015 to 0.034), corresponding to a 39.1 hr doubling time.
source: Here, the median growth constant was 0.018 hour−1 (interquartile range 0.0015 to 0.034), corresponding to a 39.1 hr doubling time.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The difference in Mtb growth between IFNγ treated and untreated MDM was not statistically significant (p=0.45).
source: However, this difference was not statistically significant (p=0.45 for treated versus untreated MDM, and p=0.16 for alveolar versus untreated MDM, Kruskal-Wallis rank sum test corrected for multiple hypotheses).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: The difference in Mtb growth between alveolar macrophages and untreated MDM was not statistically significant (p=0.16).
source: However, this difference was not statistically significant (p=0.45 for treated versus untreated MDM, and p=0.16 for alveolar versus untreated MDM, Kruskal-Wallis rank sum test corrected for multiple hypotheses).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: The growth of Mtb in dead cells seemed to be relatively independent of cellular activation and tissue source.
source: Hence, the growth of Mtb in dead cells seemed to be relatively independent of cellular activation and tissue source.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of significant differences between different cell types and activation states.

claim: Frequency of cell death after internalization of dead infected cells was 89%.
source: Frequency of cell death was 89% (Figure 8).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8.

claim: There was a strong correlation between the time of internalization and death of the internalizing cell (R2 = 0.93, p=8×10−23).
source: There was a strong correlation between the time of internalization and death of the internalizing cell (R2 = 0.93, p=8×10−23, Figure 8—figure supplement 1), with a median time to death of 3.2 hr (interquartile range of 1.5 to 6.0 hr).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: The median time to death after internalization of dead infected cells was 3.2 hr (interquartile range of 1.5 to 6.0 hr).
source: There was a strong correlation between the time of internalization and death of the internalizing cell (R2 = 0.93, p=8×10−23, Figure 8—figure supplement 1), with a median time to death of 3.2 hr (interquartile range of 1.5 to 6.0 hr).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: Dead infected cells contained a median of 114 Mtb.
source: We compared the frequency of death from dead cell pickups to the frequency of death in cells internalizing large cell-free aggregates (81–300 bacilli), which had a similar median number of bacteria (dead infected cells contained a median of 114 Mtb, versus 125 Mtb for cell-free aggregates).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claim: Cell-free aggregates (81–300 bacilli) contained a median of 125 Mtb.
source: We compared the frequency of death from dead cell pickups to the frequency of death in cells internalizing large cell-free aggregates (81–300 bacilli), which had a similar median number of bacteria (dead infected cells contained a median of 114 Mtb, versus 125 Mtb for cell-free aggregates).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claim: Death frequency was 81% for cells that internalized cell-free aggregates.
source: Death frequency was 81% for cells that internalized cell-free aggregates, and the difference between death frequencies was not significant (p=0.16).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claim: The difference between death frequencies from dead cell pickups versus cell-free aggregates was not significant (p=0.16).
source: Death frequency was 81% for cells that internalized cell-free aggregates, and the difference between death frequencies was not significant (p=0.16).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: The highly cytotoxic effect of dead infected cell internalization can be mostly explained by the high number of Mtb they contain.
source: This indicated that the highly cytotoxic effect of dead infected cell internalization can be mostly explained by the high number of Mtb they contain.
evidence: This is inferred from the similar death frequencies between dead cell pickups and large cell-free aggregates with similar bacterial numbers.

claim: Only the one day doubling time in dead cells resulted in high Mtb growth over the simulation period of 60 days.
source: Strikingly, only the one day doubling time in dead cells resulted in high Mtb growth over the simulation period of 60 days (Figure 9B, right panels).
evidence: This is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 9B.

claim: High Mtb growth was very sensitive to the doubling time.
source: High Mtb growth was very sensitive to the doubling time (Figure 9—figure supplement 1), and this could not be explained by the differences in doubling time if growth was cell-free (Figure 9B, white lines in right panels), as both growth rates were rapid for the timescale of the simulations.
evidence: This is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1.

claim: The fraction of simulations reaching 1000 or more Mtb within 60 days was 0.21 for a one day doubling time and 0.0003 for a two day doubling time.
source: The fraction of simulations reaching 1000 or more Mtb within 60 days was 0.21 for a one day doubling time and 0.0003 for a two day doubling time (code provided as Source code 3).
evidence: This is supported by simulation results.

claim: Faster Mtb growth in the dead cell leads to larger intracellular clumps upon phagocytosis by another cell, and hence to a higher probability of death of the phagocytosing cell.
source: Rather, this simplified simulation shows the presence of positive feedback in the host cell-Mtb interactions: faster Mtb growth in the dead cell leads to larger intracellular clumps upon phagocytosis by another cell, and hence to a higher probability of death of the phagocytosing cell, leading to Mtb growth in the new dead cell and a higher probability to kill the next phagocyte in the infection chain.
evidence: This is inferred from the simulation results showing positive feedback dynamics.

claim: High Mtb concentrations have been reported in vivo upon examination of the cavity surface in human tuberculous granulomas.
source: While in general Mtb bacilli are hard to find in intact closed granulomas (Lin et al., 2014), high Mtb concentrations have been reported in vivo upon examination of the cavity surface in human tuberculous granulomas (Hunter, 2011; Hunter et al., 2007; Welsh et al., 2011) as well as cavity containing granulomas in rabbits infected with experimental pulmonary TB (Kaplan et al., 2003), and the cavity surface of granulomas with a necrotic core in the granuloma-forming Kramnik mouse model (Irwin et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to the literature.

claim: Histologic examination has shown clumped bacteria as well as highly infected macrophages at the luminal surface of cavities in areas with extensive cellular necrosis.
source: Histologic examination has shown clumped bacteria as well as highly infected macrophages at the luminal surface of cavities in areas with extensive cellular necrosis (Kaplan et al., 2003; Hunter, 2011; Irwin et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to the literature.

claim: Mtb naturally aggregate, unless cultured with a nonionic detergent such as Tween 80.
source: Mtb naturally aggregate, unless cultured with a nonionic detergent such as Tween 80 (Dubos and Middlebrook, 1948).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Dubos and Middlebrook, 1948.

claim: The protective effect of efferocytosis may occur when cells die by apoptosis and the number of bacilli inside the dead cell is small while the number of uninfected macrophages is large.
source: However, the protective effect of efferocytosis may occur when cells die by apoptosis and the number of bacilli inside the dead cell is small while the number of uninfected macrophages is large, enabling the surrounding macrophages to divide up the bacillary load of a single dead infected cell.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about the conditions under which efferocytosis is protective.

claim: Mtb can inhibit phagosome-lysosome fusion and complete phagosome acidification.
source: Mtb can inhibit phagosome-lysosome fusion and complete phagosome acidification (Vergne et al., 2003; Rohde et al., 2007; Via et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to the literature.

claim: Acidification may occur when macrophages are activated with cytokines such GM-CSF.
source: However, acidification may occur when macrophages are activated with cytokines such GM-CSF (Denis and Ghadirian, 1990), as are the MDMs used for this study.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Denis and Ghadirian, 1990.

claim: Mtb growth may be impaired or arrested in acidified vacuoles.
source: In this case, Mtb growth may be impaired or arrested in acidified vacuoles (Gomes et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Gomes et al., 1999.

claim: T cells control Mtb by activating macrophages to kill Mtb through IFNγ secretion.
source: T cells control Mtb by activating macrophages to kill Mtb through IFNγ secretion (Flynn et al., 1993), and CD8+ cytotoxic T cells target intracellular bacteria by granulysin release (Stenger et al., 1998), which has been reported to enable granzymes to enter and kill the bacteria (Walch et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to the literature.

claim: CD8+ cytotoxic T cells target intracellular bacteria by granulysin release.
source: T cells control Mtb by activating macrophages to kill Mtb through IFNγ secretion (Flynn et al., 1993), and CD8+ cytotoxic T cells target intracellular bacteria by granulysin release (Stenger et al., 1998), which has been reported to enable granzymes to enter and kill the bacteria (Walch et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to the literature.

claim: Granulysin has been reported to enable granzymes to enter and kill the bacteria.
source: T cells control Mtb by activating macrophages to kill Mtb through IFNγ secretion (Flynn et al., 1993), and CD8+ cytotoxic T cells target intracellular bacteria by granulysin release (Stenger et al., 1998), which has been reported to enable granzymes to enter and kill the bacteria (Walch et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Walch et al., 2014.

claim: T cell mechanisms would be restricted by the Mtb mediated death of the host cell before recognition and targeting by T cells.
source: These mechanisms would counteract the spread of Mtb, but would likely be restricted by the Mtb mediated death of the host cell before recognition and targeting by T cells, limited T cell effector function in the granuloma (Egen et al., 2011), lack of T cells in the inner cell layer of granulomas (Ulrichs et al., 2004), and impaired expression of perforin and granulysin observed in Mtb granulomas (Andersson et al., 2007).
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about factors that would limit T cell effectiveness.

claim: There is a lack of T cells in the inner cell layer of granulomas.
